explanations: terra: Prayer is heavy except for the humble, locating the decisive difference in the worshipper's inward posture rather than the visible act; 2:46 states their awareness of meeting God.
terra: The humble pray with certainty that they will meet and return to their Lord, supplying the remembered divine horizon absent from performative prayer.
terra: The covenant places kindness to orphans and the needy beside prayer and almsgiving, an early formulation of the duties the section shows splitting apart.
terra: Believers are told to pardon and overlook hostile conduct for a time, directing restraint toward offense rather than toward the needs the section says must remain visible.
terra: “Remember Me; I will remember you” is the positive reciprocity opposite both 9:67's forgetting and the desire to secure remembrance from human spectators.

terra: Righteousness is located beyond outward orientation in giving loved wealth to orphans and the needy, establishing prayer, and fulfilling commitments; it joins all the section's separated duties.

terra: A person's worldly speech impresses the listener and he invokes God concerning his heart, while the verse identifies him as fiercely contentious; attractive surface and corrupt inward reality split apart.
terra: Once the impressive speaker of 2:204 turns away, he destroys crops and living stock, showing how a bright public face can conceal conduct that removes others' provision.
terra: Worldly life is beautified for disbelievers and they mock believers, showing visible attraction converting into contempt for those whose worth is less worldly.
terra: When asked what to spend, the answer names orphans and the needy, making the easily delayed recipient part of the question's immediate field.

luna: Asked about orphans, the answer favors reforming their affairs and treats them as kin when lives are joined; this gives practical form to seeing rather than neglecting them. | terra: Reform of orphans' affairs is declared best and mixing with them is framed as living with brothers, replacing detached neglect with sustained attention.
terra: After allowing one party to waive a marital due, “do not forget graciousness between you” separates merciful relinquishment from forgetting another person's good.
terra: Guarding all prayers and standing devoutly before God gives a concise positive command against negligence about prayer.
terra: Spending followed by neither reminder nor injury preserves the recipient's dignity and keeps generosity from becoming a public claim on another person.
terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, joining care with the right kind of overlooking and rejecting aid that becomes another shove.

luna: A giver who spends to be seen by people loses the deed's fruit; the rain-washed bare rock makes display without lasting benefit a concrete reversal of the section's visible shine and missing aid. | terra: Charity done رئاء الناس joins aid to the needful with the desire to be seen, and its denial of God and the Last Day recalls how the whole surah roots both failures in denial of judgment.
terra: Those who spend seeking God's pleasure and from inner certainty are the inward opposite of 2:264's performer; the fruitful garden also contrasts with the performer's bare rock.
terra: Believers must not select inferior goods for charity that they themselves would take only with eyes closed; sight, the recipient's due, and defective giving meet concretely.

luna: The verse says that giving alms openly is good but giving them secretly to the poor is better; it distinguishes genuine care from the section's wish to shine before people. | terra: Concealed charity to the poor is called better, marking a precise boundary between an act hidden from human eyes and one done for their eyes.

terra: In the charity passage, spending is to seek God's face and returns as good to the giver; this supplies the proper audience for aid between 2:271's hidden charity and 2:273's easily missed poor.

luna: The needy may look rich because of restraint, while their marks let a careful observer recognize them; this gives the section's faint-star image a precise human counterpart: hidden need can be passed over by the casual eye. | terra: The restrained poor are mistakenly thought rich and must be recognized by their mark; this directly explains how a needy person can disappear under an untrained gaze.
terra: Spending night and day, secretly and openly, makes consistency rather than visibility the measure of care.
terra: Human desires are beautified through conspicuous forms of wealth and status, then identified as temporary worldly enjoyment, explaining how the eye is recruited by brightness.
terra: People do not attain deep goodness until they spend from what they love, ensuring that care gives the overlooked person something other than what the giver would rather not see.
terra: Spending in ease and hardship is joined to restraining anger and pardoning people, so aid and the section's right kind of overlooking another's fault meet in one character.
terra: The Prophet is told to pardon the companions, seek forgiveness for them, and continue consulting them, a concrete Quranic form of overlooking another's lapse well.
terra: What the stingy withhold from God's bounty becomes a collar around them, turning the closed hand's hidden omission into a visible burden.
terra: People who love praise for what they did not do exemplify the urge to remain conspicuous in others' eyes even when the inward deed is missing.

luna: Guardians must give orphans their property and not consume it with their own; this specifies a material form of the neglect and exploitation behind the source's account of withheld care. | terra: Giving orphans their property and forbidding substitution or absorption of it prevents the guardian's appetite from making the child's right disappear.

luna: The verse warns against failing to deal justly with orphan girls under guardianship; it makes overlooked vulnerability a reason to limit the guardian's power. | terra: Fear of failing justice toward orphan girls changes what marriage choices are permitted, so the orphan's otherwise weak position governs the stronger person's conduct.

luna: Within the adjacent orphan-property instructions in 4:2–6, this verse requires provision, clothing, and kind speech for dependents whose property is being guarded; its own contribution is care during guardianship. | terra: Guardians must maintain, clothe, and speak kindly to vulnerable property-holders; within the orphan passage leading to 4:6, care is continuous rather than postponed to the final transfer.

luna: Guardians test orphans until marriageable age and hand over their property only on finding sound judgment; the verse makes the source's “good comes late” dictionary gloss concrete as protection lasting until maturity. | terra: Orphans are tested until maturity, their property then handed over, and guardians forbidden to consume it hastily; it distinguishes protective delay from the section's negligent delay of goodness.

luna: When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an inheritance division, they are to receive provision and kind words; the scene puts overlooked dependents in view at the moment wealth is apportioned. | terra: If orphans and needy people are present at an estate division, they must receive provision and kind speech; physical presence must lead to notice rather than exclusion.
terra: Those who fear leaving weak offspring behind must fear God and speak rightly, making imagined parental absence a reason to keep vulnerable children present in one's moral sight.

luna: Those who unjustly consume orphan property are said to consume fire; the sharp warning exposes the harm hidden by treating the orphan's property as available. | terra: Those who consume orphan property are said to consume fire into their bellies, revealing the grave reality hidden behind an easy act of appropriation.
terra: Kindness to orphans and the needy is commanded beside worship of God, while proud self-display is rejected at the verse's end.
terra: Stinginess, urging others to stinginess, and hiding God's bounty expose the closed hand beside 4:36's orphan and needy and 4:38's ostentatious spender.

luna: It condemns spending wealth to be seen by people while disbelieving in God and the Last Day; this directly matches the section's account of people seeking visibility while neglecting real care. | terra: Spending only to be seen by people makes public brightness itself corrupt the act that should have reached another, precisely the section's reversal of attention.
terra: God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good, fixing the moral worth of what human eyes may dismiss as negligible.
terra: The intoxicated may not approach prayer until they know what they are saying; awareness of one's words marks a concrete boundary against absent-minded worship.
terra: People who present themselves as pure are corrected by God's sole authority to purify, limiting the self-fashioned brightness used to claim notice.

luna: It raises the rights of orphan girls whom guardians fail to give their due; this is a specific instance of the neglect attached to the source's orphan image. | terra: Orphan women are denied what is prescribed for them while others desire to marry them, and the command is to stand for orphans in justice; desire here makes the vulnerable person's right disappear from view.

luna: The hypocrites rise to prayer lazily, perform for people, and remember God only a little; this closely joins the section's heartless prayer to its account of trying to be seen. | terra: The hypocrites stand for prayer lazily, seek human notice in يراؤون الناس, and remember God only a little; it gathers absent-hearted prayer and the refusal to be overlooked into one scene.
terra: Despite repeated betrayal, the Prophet is told to pardon and overlook; another's fault, rather than a vulnerable person's claim, becomes the proper object of deliberate passing over.
terra: Intoxicants and gambling are said to turn people away from God's remembrance and from prayer, naming concrete attractions that make the heart depart from worship.
terra: The Messenger must not drive away inconspicuous people who call on their Lord morning and evening seeking His face; sincere worshippers must remain visible despite elite pressure.
terra: The elite ask whether these lowly believers are really those God favored, exposing the status-based misreading that motivates the forbidden expulsion in 6:52.
terra: After the prohibition on driving away lowly worshippers in 6:52, God commands that those who come believing be greeted with peace and mercy, replacing exclusion with direct welcome.
terra: God knows the falling leaf and the grain in the earth's darkness, giving the section's hidden small object a witness who never passes over it.
terra: Abraham sees a star and then rejects it when it sets; the link is limited to a visible celestial object disappearing, but it cautions against attaching ultimate worth to what captures sight.

luna: It likewise forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, turning attention toward a vulnerable right that can otherwise be missed. | terra: The orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity, requiring sustained guardianship through the very interval named in the section's definition.
terra: Those distracted by worldly life and treating religion as play are forgotten as they forgot the meeting of the Day, linking attractive distraction to reciprocal abandonment.

luna: This verse joins hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear with being heedless; it gives a bodily image for the section's eye missing the faint and heart absent from prayer. | terra: Hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear converge in the designation الغافلون, closely matching the section's joined failures of eye and heart.
terra: Accepting what is easy, commanding right, and turning away from the ignorant supplies a disciplined form of passing over offense rather than passing over need.
terra: Quiet, humble remembrance morning and evening ends with the command not to be among the heedless, setting sustained inward attention against سهو.
terra: True believers' hearts tremble when God is mentioned and their faith increases on hearing His signs; 8:3 then carries this living heart into prayer and giving.
terra: Those inwardly moved in 8:2 establish prayer and spend from God's provision, reversing both the empty prayer and withheld aid of the section.
terra: The divine allocation of spoils assigns a share to orphans and the needy, formally preventing their claims from depending on whether powerful people happen to notice them.

luna: This verse joins prayer performed lazily with spending done reluctantly; that pairing makes visible the same neglect of worship and withheld aid developed in the section. | terra: The hypocrites come to prayer lazily and spend unwillingly, another direct joining of depleted worship with reluctant aid.
terra: Immediately after hypocritical prayer and spending in 9:54, the command not to be impressed by their wealth or children disciplines the gaze that their outward advantages capture.
terra: Obligatory alms are assigned to the poor and needy among named recipients, institutionally keeping those easily missed within the community's field of obligation.

luna: The hypocrites “close their hands” and forget God, so He forgets them; the verse directly joins withheld help to reciprocal forgetting, as the section does. | terra: The hypocrites close their hands, forget God, and are consequently forgotten; bodily withholding and reciprocal neglect expose what the section's heedlessness looks like from outside.
terra: Some covenant that if God gives bounty they will give charity and be righteous; 9:76-77 expose what happens when promised care is displaced by self-concern.
terra: Once bounty arrives, they become stingy and turn away, changing provision into the closed hand rather than the charity promised in 9:75.
terra: Their broken promise and lies leave hypocrisy in their hearts until meeting God, connecting withheld giving to an inward corruption that outlasts the public pledge.
terra: Hypocrites ridicule both willing donors and believers able to give only their effort, so the socially small gift and giver are passed over precisely because they do not glitter.
terra: The repeated command not to be impressed by hypocrites' wealth and children confirms that their visible advantages are a recurring danger to moral sight.
terra: A mosque is built for harm while its builders swear they intended good; even a visible worship structure can become a display masking a contrary heart.
terra: A mosque founded on mindfulness and inhabited by people who love purification is the positive boundary against the deceptive worship structure of 9:107.
terra: Not even an atom's weight, smaller or greater, escapes the Lord while people act; divine attention thus includes what human scale calls too small to see.
terra: Noah's chiefs dismiss his followers as the lowest people at first glance, a direct account of sight converting low social brightness into false lack of worth.
terra: Noah refuses to drive away the believers and grounds their worth in meeting their Lord, reversing the hand that pushes the socially disregarded person aside.
terra: Noah asks who could protect him from God if he drove the believers away, giving divine weight to his refusal in 11:29 to erase the lowly from the gathering.
terra: Noah refuses to say that God will give no good to those whom the chiefs' eyes despise; it explicitly separates low visibility in elite eyes from worth before God and continues 11:27-30.
terra: Joseph's brothers resent that he is more present in their father's love, exposing the competition not to be overlooked that precedes their removal of another child.
terra: They propose killing or expelling Joseph so their father's face will be exclusively theirs; this is the section's dynamic of seeking the gaze by making another disappear.
terra: Casting the child into the hidden bottom of a well turns jealous competition for attention into a physical act of removal, as 12:9 proposed.
terra: Jacob fears the wolf may take Joseph while the brothers are heedless of him, a direct child-and-guardian scene in which lapse of attention becomes danger.
terra: The brothers actually place Joseph in the hidden well, completing 12:9-10's plan to gain attention by removing a child from sight.

terra: After Joseph has been cast away and sold, his Egyptian purchaser orders that his lodging be honored and considers taking him as a son; the discarded child is deliberately restored to a household's care.
terra: A requested act of mention is forgotten and Joseph consequently remains in prison for several years; it concretely joins being forgotten to the delayed arrival of good.
terra: Jacob's eyes whiten with grief while he keeps naming the absent Joseph, a poignant reversal of the child who disappears because no guardian continues to hold him in sight and heart.
terra: Hearts find rest in God's remembrance, presenting remembrance as the heart's settled presence rather than its departure from prayer.
terra: Prayer and spending secretly and openly are commanded together before the day when social exchange cannot repair neglect.
terra: The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward worldly enjoyments and instead to lower his wing to believers, joining disciplined sight to gentle care for those easily passed over.
terra: Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due names provision as an owed right, not a favor that may be postponed until the vulnerable person is noticed.

luna: The instruction not to keep one's hand chained to one's neck warns against a closed-handed extreme; it makes the section's withholding of even small help legible as a failure of giving. | terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor opened without limit; the chained-hand image explains the embodied stinginess named in 9:67.

luna: The command not to approach an orphan's property except for its best use until maturity guards the child through the separation described by the source's ي ت م definition. | terra: Protection of orphan property until maturity keeps the fatherless child's future continuously before the guardian rather than letting good arrive too late.
terra: Earth's adornment is made a test of who is best in deed, so visible beauty is a field of moral testing rather than proof of the viewer's or object's worth.

luna: The command “do not let your eyes pass beyond them” protects humble worshippers from being overlooked for worldly adornment; the verse also describes a heart heedless of remembrance, reversing the section's gaze toward brightness and heart gone from prayer. | terra: The command ولا تعد عيناك عنهم forbids the eye to pass beyond inconspicuous worshippers toward worldly adornment, while أغفلنا قلبه names the heedless heart; this directly stages the section's gaze and heart.
terra: Wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better with God; this corrects the eye that follows what shines now.
terra: The record leaves neither small nor great uncounted, reversing the human habit of letting the inconspicuous thing disappear.
terra: Moses asks not to be taken to task for what he forgot, giving a concrete interpersonal setting in which a lapse can be passed over without erasing a duty or a vulnerable person.

terra: The damaged boat belongs to poor workers and is marred to save it from a king seizing every sound vessel, an indirect scene in which unobtrusive protection preserves the poor person's provision.

luna: The wall is repaired to preserve treasure for two orphans until maturity because their father was righteous; protection continues across paternal absence, reversing the orphan left without someone to keep him in view. | terra: A treasure is preserved for two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous; divine care carries delayed good to children whose father can no longer guard it.
terra: One who hopes to meet the Lord must do right and associate no one in the Lord's worship, excluding a human audience from the act's governing intention.
terra: Successors who أضاعوا الصلاة and follow desires embody negligence directed at prayer itself, rather than a mere accidental lapse within it.
terra: وما كان ربك نسيا states that the Lord is never forgetful, distinguishing divine delay from the human neglect through which the orphan is named.
terra: أقم الصلاة لذكري defines prayer as remembrance of God, the direct inward opposite of a heart gone away from its prayer.
terra: The infant Moses is sent onto the river yet formed “under My eye”; separation from parental sight is met by God's unbroken guardianship.
terra: Moses is returned to his mother so her eye may be comforted, making restored human watchfulness part of the divine care announced in 20:39.
terra: Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets, setting divine knowledge against both the eye that misses the small and the heart that leaves its prayer.
terra: Turning away from God's remembrance begins the sequence that ends in 20:126 with blindness and being forgotten, giving the section's departed heart a trajectory.
terra: The resurrected person asks why he has been raised blind though he once saw, making failed spiritual attention visible before 20:126 explains it as forgetting the signs.
terra: The one who forgot God's signs is himself left forgotten and blind, completing 20:124-25's movement from turning away to loss of sight.

luna: The warning not to extend one's eyes toward worldly adornment gives a specific counter-direction to the section's eye drawn to brightness and its people trying to shine. | terra: The eye must not stretch toward the flower of worldly life given to others; God's provision is declared better and more lasting, correcting the gaze that equates brightness with value.
luna: The next verse commands the Prophet's household to maintain prayer and promises that God provides; it completes 20:131's warning about worldly adornment with prayer and reliance on provision.
luna: People's accounting has drawn near while they turn away heedlessly; the source's gloss of neglect links this to the surah-wide denial of judgment that lets the orphan and prayer be disregarded.
terra: Even a mustard-seed weight is brought into the perfectly just balance, another assurance that smallness never removes a deed or claim from divine reckoning.
terra: Pilgrims are commanded to eat from sacrificial animals and feed the afflicted poor, making the needy person's food an explicit part of worship.
terra: Humble hearts at God's mention, steadfastness, established prayer, and spending are held together, showing the heart, worship, and care as one response.
terra: The sacrificial animals are provision from God, and people are again commanded to feed both the contented and the petitioner; ritual remembrance issues in shared food.

luna: The successful believers are humble in their prayers, a direct positive counterpart to the section's prayer from which the heart has gone. | terra: Believers are humble and inwardly present in their prayer, supplying the positive posture opposed to ساهون عن صلاتهم.
terra: Careful preservation of prayers directly reverses treating them as something the heart can leave unattended.

luna: The source's dictionary gives س ه و a secondary sense of graciously overlooking another's slip; this verse commands pardon and overlooking, a deliberate, merciful kind of not noticing unlike neglect of the orphan or one's prayer. | terra: The well-provided are told not to withhold from needy kin and also to pardon and overlook; it unites giving with the section's “good” kind of overlooking another's lapse.

luna: The lamp's glass is likened to a brilliant star; this joins the section's star imagery to a striking, visible light, the opposite pole of the faint star overlooked among brighter ones. | terra: The lamp whose glass is like a brilliantly shining star is a deliberate celestial reversal of the section's nearly missed Suha; 24:36-37 then locates that light in remembrance and undistracted prayer.
terra: The star-like lamp of 24:35 is placed in houses where God's name is remembered morning and evening, and 24:37 identifies people whose prayer is not distracted by trade.
terra: Trade and sale do not distract these people from remembrance, prayer, or almsgiving; it directly reverses the departed heart and joins attended prayer to open-handed care.
terra: The servants of the Merciful spend without extravagance or stinginess, marking measured generosity as the boundary opposite a hand simply closed to need.
terra: The chiefs object that the lowest people follow Noah, making social rank the brightness by which they decide whom to notice.
terra: Noah asks what knowledge he has of his lowly followers' prior deeds, refusing the elite premise in 26:111 that visible class licenses judgment; 26:113 assigns their account to God.
terra: Noah places his followers' account with his Lord, refusing the elite demand to judge their worth by the visible social measure raised in 26:111.
terra: Noah says he will not drive away the believers, directly reversing the section's shove against the vulnerable and the elite wish to erase the lowly.
terra: Moses' mother is told to cast her infant into the river when afraid, yet promised his return; extreme separation from parental sight remains enclosed by divine attention.
terra: Pharaoh's household picks the floating infant up, supplying the concrete human discovery between his mother's separation in 28:7 and the woman's protective speech in 28:9.
terra: Pharaoh's wife calls the found infant a comfort of the eye, forbids killing him, and imagines care or adoption, reversing the impulse to remove a vulnerable child from view.
terra: Moses' mother's heart becomes emptied and nearly discloses him until God strengthens it; involuntary anguish over a child out of sight contrasts with a heart casually leaving prayer.
terra: Moses' sister follows him and watches from a distance while others do not perceive, a child-protection scene built from sustained, unobtrusive sight.
terra: Returning Moses to his mother so her eye is comforted reverses the section's image of a child left without the gaze that keeps him present.
terra: The steadfast repel evil with good and spend from their provision; right forbearance and open-handed care appear together rather than being misdirected toward neglect.
terra: Qarun's oppressive wealth is so conspicuous that even its keys burden a group; it prepares the public display of 28:79 and shows how sheer abundance announces itself.
terra: Qarun goes out in his adornment and spectators desire his visible fortune, a full scene of brightness capturing the eye and defining worth.
terra: People given knowledge answer the spectators of 28:79 that God's reward is better, explicitly correcting desire awakened by Qarun's adornment.
terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed after the display of 28:79, making the object that monopolized attention disappear beneath the earth.
terra: The previous day's admirers recognize that worldly expansion is no proof of divine favor, revising the gaze that Qarun's glitter had captured.
terra: Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing and God's remembrance is greater; its moral work exposes the emptiness of a prayer abandoned by its heart.
terra: Giving the needy and traveler their due is declared best for those seeking God's face, joining care to the right audience rather than public display.
terra: Giving alms while seeking God's face is contrasted with increase sought through other people's wealth, separating God-directed care from self-amplification through others.
terra: Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in a rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God; what is tiny and concealed never escapes divine attention.
terra: Turning one's cheek from people and walking boastfully are forbidden, correcting the bodily performance by which a person enlarges himself while diminishing those before him.
terra: “Taste, because you forgot the meeting of this day; We have forgotten you” turns chosen inattention into the very exclusion the negligent person failed to fear.
terra: Children are to be called by their fathers, and those whose fathers are unknown are treated as brothers and protected associates, preserving relation where paternal identity is absent.
terra: Nothing as small as an atom, nor smaller or larger, escapes the Lord; the tiny concealed thing remains fully present to divine knowledge.
terra: Reciting God's book, establishing prayer, and spending secretly and openly describe worship whose inward remembrance issues in care.
terra: The refusal “Should we feed one whom God could feed?” gives speech to the exact evasion by which the poor person's food is left out.
terra: Woe to hearts hardened against God's remembrance defines the inward failure behind worship that remains only an exterior act.
terra: God knows the furtive glance and what breasts conceal, holding both the wandering eye and the absent or performative heart within divine sight.
terra: Withholding alms is placed beside disbelief in the hereafter, closely paralleling the surah's movement from denial of judgment to withheld small aid.
terra: Repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into a close friend, a Quranic enactment of the section's good social conduct that passes over another's lapse rather than another's need.
terra: Those who avoid major sins forgive when angry, identifying the fault of another as a proper object of deliberate overlooking.
terra: One may answer harm equally, but pardon joined to repair has its reward with God, distinguishing fruitful overlooking from negligent omission.
terra: Objectors ask why the Quran was not sent to a great man from one of the two towns, openly treating visible social prominence as the measure of who merits revelation.
terra: God rejects their attempt to distribute His mercy and says His mercy is better than what they accumulate, correcting the prestige-based gaze voiced in 43:31.
terra: Silver roofs and ascending stairs are imagined for unbelieving houses, deliberately heightening the visible splendor that 43:35 reduces to temporary worldly enjoyment.
terra: Doors and couches extend the glittering house scene of 43:33, supplying the social surfaces whose value 43:35 sharply limits.
terra: All the gold and ornament of 43:33-34 are only worldly enjoyment, while the hereafter belongs to the mindful; brightness and durable worth are explicitly separated.
terra: Pharaoh points his people to his kingdom and the rivers beneath him and asks whether they see, deliberately using visible splendor to monopolize judgment before belittling Moses in 43:52.
terra: Pharaoh calls Moses contemptible and barely articulate while comparing him with his own spectacle, a direct instance of the glittering figure making the quieter one seem negligible.
terra: Pharaoh demands gold bracelets or accompanying angels as visible credentials for Moses, exposing the expectation that truth must shine conspicuously to receive notice.
terra: Pharaoh makes light of his people and they obey him, showing the social effect of the visual prestige and belittling comparison he staged in 43:51-53.
terra: Being forgotten on the Day because one forgot its meeting makes neglect reciprocal, as in 9:67, and reveals the final consequence of wanting human notice while ignoring God.
terra: The question whether people reflect on the Quran or have locks on their hearts gives a bodily image for attention that cannot enter.
terra: When called to spend, some withhold, and the verse says their stinginess recoils on themselves; refusing another person's claim damages the one who overlooks it.
terra: People forbidden to ridicule others are reminded that those who look lesser may be better; visible rank is therefore an unreliable measure of worth.
terra: The reminder benefits one who has a heart, gives ear, and is حاضر as a witness; these are the precise faculties missing when the heart has gone from what stands before it.
terra: The curse on the conjecturers identifies who the ساهون of 51:11 are; its own contribution is to connect engulfing heedlessness with confident speech unsupported by knowledge.

luna: The same source-section root س ه و appears in سَاهُونَ: here the heedless are “in a cover” of heedlessness, giving the section's missed prayer a scene of being submerged from awareness. | terra: The exact form الذين هم في غمرة ساهون places the سهو root inside an engulfing غمرة, giving the section's absent heart a surrounding medium that covers it.
terra: A recognized share in the God-conscious person's wealth belongs to the asker and deprived, filling the section's conspicuous blank where the poor person's food should be.

luna: The source's dictionary calls a rare single pearl “yetim”; here attendants are likened to a pearl kept hidden, making concealment compatible with preciousness. | terra: Attendants compared to protected pearls repeat the Quranic association of hiddenness with value, countering the section's human habit of noticing only exposed brilliance.
terra: The command not to present oneself as pure because God best knows the mindful undercuts the performer's attempt to control how others see him.

luna: The source's “single, rare pearl” dictionary sense meets the Qur'an's image of a hidden pearl: what is out of sight may still be precious, as with the overlooked orphan. | terra: The comparison to protected, hidden pearls gives Quranic dignity to value not exposed to the casual gaze, reversing the assumption that what remains unseen lacks brilliance.
terra: The call for believers' hearts to become humble at God's remembrance confronts the hardened or departed heart rather than merely correcting an outward posture.
terra: Worldly life is described as amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before its vegetation withers, exposing why bright display is a poor guide to lasting value.
terra: Those who are stingy and command others to stinginess reproduce the same social failure as refusing to urge feeding the needy.
terra: Satan makes a people forget God's remembrance, identifying the active capture of attention that leaves the heart absent from its proper object.

luna: The verse directs a share of distributed wealth to orphans and the needy so it does not circulate only among the rich; this counters the section's neglected vulnerable person and withheld provision. | terra: Orphans and the needy receive a share so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, directly countering a social gaze and flow captured by the already prominent.
terra: The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need, reversing the self-centering gaze and closed hand that let the orphan and poor person vanish.
terra: Those who forget God are made to forget themselves; negligence of the highest object hollows out the negligent person, as the section's prayer loses its own heart.
terra: At the call to Friday prayer believers must leave trade; 62:11 shows the exact failure when visible commerce draws them away.
terra: After prayer, seeking provision is permitted while abundant remembrance continues; this marks the boundary that 62:11 crosses when commerce becomes a visual diversion from worship.
terra: When people see trade or amusement they scatter toward it and leave the Messenger standing, literally staging the eye's attraction to the bright diversion as worship is abandoned.

terra: The hypocrites' bodies impress the eye and their speech draws the ear, yet they are like propped timber; it is a precise portrait of shining enough to avoid being overlooked while inward life is absent.

luna: The hypocrites urge others not to spend on those with God's Messenger; this is a concrete withholding of provision from a vulnerable group, parallel to the section's neglected food and small aid. | terra: The hypocrites explicitly tell others not to spend on the people around the Messenger so that they disperse, weaponizing withheld provision to make the lowly disappear.
terra: Wealth and children must not distract believers from God's remembrance; the verse names the attractive objects that can draw the heart away.

luna: The source's secondary dictionary sense of س ه و is graciously overlooking another's lapse; this verse tells believers to pardon, overlook, and forgive family members who have wronged them, a merciful use of overlooking unlike neglect. | terra: Believers facing hostility within their families are told that pardon, overlooking, and forgiveness meet God's forgiveness, concretizing the section's benign kind of inattention.
terra: The command to spend is joined to being protected from the soul's greed, locating the closed hand in an inward condition that can be overcome.
terra: Whether speech is hidden or voiced, God knows what hearts contain; concealment therefore cannot make either sincerity or neglect disappear.
terra: The Creator's subtle knowledge in 67:14 grounds 67:13's claim that hidden speech and hearts remain known.
terra: The garden owners tell one another that no poor person may enter, turning the needy person's disappearance into an explicit plan.
terra: They set out with confident power to withhold, enacting the exclusion voiced in 68:24 before the garden's loss exposes it.
terra: Failure to believe in God is immediately expressed in 69:34 as failure to urge feeding the needy, giving the neglect its inward source just as 107 links denial, prayer, and the orphan.

luna: The condemned person did not urge feeding the needy; this repeats the section's specific link between moral failure and not prompting others to provide food. | terra: ولا يحض على طعام المسكين is the same concrete failure to urge feeding found in the surah; 69:33 supplies its setting in refusal to believe in God.
terra: Constancy in prayer, introduced by 70:22, directly opposes neglect of prayer and leads in 70:24-25 to acknowledging the poor person's share.
terra: A recognized right in their wealth prepares 70:25's named recipients, making aid a due that cannot simply vanish from attention.
terra: The recognized right belongs to the asker and the deprived; beside constant prayer in 70:23, it reverses the section's pairing of negligent worship and missing provision.
terra: Those who carefully guard their prayers are the direct opposite of people whose hearts have gone away from theirs.
terra: Night worship is described as stronger in impression and firmer for speech, offering a setting of gathered attention opposed to a heart that wanders away.

luna: In the same account of what led to the Fire, they say they were not among those who prayed; this makes the section's prayer abandoned by the heart part of a stated moral pattern, not a minor lapse. | terra: The people of the Fire say they were not among those who prayed; with 74:44 it pairs failed prayer with failed care for the poor, the same moral adjacency as the section.

luna: The next confession is that they did not feed the needy, directly completing the preceding failure to pray and echoing the section's unnoticed absence of food for the poor. | terra: “We did not feed the needy” completes 74:43's confession about prayer, directly bringing the missing poor person's food beside empty or absent worship.
terra: The person neither believes nor prays; 75:33 then shows the same person walking back to his people with conspicuous swagger, linking failed worship to public self-display.
terra: After the failures of belief and prayer in 75:31-32, the person goes to his family strutting, making visible performance the exterior left when worship is absent.

luna: Those devoted to God give food they love to an orphan, a needy person, and a captive; the act directly answers the section's neglected orphan and unmentioned meal. | terra: Feeding food despite loving it to a needy person, an orphan, and a captive makes the overlooked person's due visible and enacted.

luna: Their stated motive is God's face, with no wish for recompense or thanks; this contrasts the section's people trying to be seen, and explains the feeding in 76:8. | terra: The feeders of 76:8 seek no repayment or thanks, so their care is governed by God's face rather than the human gaze sought by those who show off.
terra: The youths are seen as scattered pearls, a visible and numerous pearl image that forms a deliberate opposite pole to the section's single pearl missed in its shell.
luna: The stars are blotted out at the Judgment; this cosmic loss of visibility sharpens the section's image of a small star already hard to see.
terra: The frown opens the incident completed in 80:10: attention registers the less prestigious visitor as an interruption before his hidden worth is disclosed.
terra: The blind man is the one who came, making the episode's overlooked figure someone whose lack of sight sharpens the moral failure of others' sight.
terra: The overlooked visitor may purify himself; the verse exposes value invisible to the surface judgment dramatized in 80:1-2.
terra: The possibility that reminder may benefit the blind visitor continues 80:3 and shows what is lost when attention passes him over.
terra: The self-sufficient man is the socially bright pole of the scene, receiving attention that 80:10 says was withheld from the striving visitor.
terra: Directing one's attention to the self-sufficient person concretely stages the gaze going where prestige already shines.
terra: The addressee is not accountable if the self-sufficient man refuses purification, removing the excuse for privileging him over the striving visitor of 80:8-10.
terra: The other man comes striving, giving the person passed over in 80:10 an active sincerity that outward status had concealed.
terra: His reverent fear supplies the hidden inward brightness missed by the social gaze in the surrounding scene.
terra: فأنت عنه تلهى makes distraction from the earnest blind visitor the climax of 80:1-9, a concrete case of attention passing over the less socially dazzling person.
luna: The stars are dimmed in this end-time scene; it reverses the ordinary field of bright stars among which the source's faint Suha goes unnoticed.

luna: The oath begins with the retreating stars; the next verse describes the runners that hide, making celestial withdrawal a specific parallel to the source's hard-to-see Suha. | terra: The oath by celestial bodies that withdraw begins a Quranic sky scene in which apparent disappearance, completed by their movement in 81:16, remains divinely marked.

luna: The “running, hiding” heavenly bodies complete 81:15's retreating stars and parallel the source's faint star that disappears from an observer's notice. | terra: The moving bodies that hide continue 81:15's oath, offering a celestial analogue to the section's small star slipping from ordinary sight.

luna: The “piercing star” is the conspicuous opposite of the tiny faint Suha in the source section, clarifying how brightness draws the eye. | terra: النجم الثاقب is the piercingly visible star, the opposite pole to the section's tiny hidden Suha and therefore a check on treating visibility as worth.
terra: Remembering the Lord's name and praying form one action, while 87:16 names preference for nearer worldly life as the competing attraction.

luna: The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” names the outward neglect that the section's dictionary gloss links to ي ت م: others fail to notice the orphan's right, unlike the commanded care. | terra: كلا بل لا تكرمون اليتيم names failure to honor the orphan, making the neglect carried in the section's dictionary account of يتيم explicit conduct.

luna: This next rebuke says they do not urge one another to feed the needy, making explicit the food-shaped absence that the section sees in 107:3; 89:17 supplies the adjacent orphan rebuke. | terra: Nor urging one another to feed the needy continues 89:17's neglected-orphan scene and closely matches the section's noticed absence of concern for طعام المسكين.
terra: The boastful spender asks in effect whether anyone has seen him; God's challenge punctures concern with human visibility by asserting an inescapable witness.

luna: The difficult ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, giving a concrete opposite to the absent food and unurged care in the section. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger is the concrete act that 90:15-16 directs toward an orphan and a person in misery.

luna: The next verse specifies an orphan who is a near relative, applying the source-section root ي ت م to one of the people fed in 90:14. | terra: An orphan of near kin is named as the recipient of the difficult ascent introduced by feeding in 90:14, making the solitary child a claim on action.

luna: The following verse names a needy person in misery, specifying whose hunger the food in 90:14 answers and completing the section's neglected-poor image. | terra: The needy person in dust completes the feeding scene of 90:14 and makes visible the low condition that the comfortable gaze can pass over.
terra: The one who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient combines the closed hand with the status posture that receives attention in the Abasa scene.
terra: The most mindful person gives wealth to purify himself, turning resources toward another rather than using another person as a mirror for reputation.
terra: No favor is being repaid in the giver's act, excluding the social transaction and applause that could govern visible generosity.
terra: Seeking only the face of the Most High supplies the direct alternative audience to showing off before people.
terra: “Your Lord has not forsaken you” frames the orphan recollection of 93:6: apparent delay and dimness do not mean abandonment by God.
terra: The later state being better than the first gives temporal shape to 93:3-6: a wait can hold promised good without meaning that the orphaned servant was forgotten.
terra: The promise that the Lord will give until the addressee is satisfied answers the section's dictionary sense of good arriving late to the orphan.

luna: The speaker recalls finding the Prophet an orphan and giving him refuge; the same ي ت م relation is answered here by shelter rather than the section's orphan-pushing. | terra: God's finding the Prophet an orphan and giving shelter reverses the child being left outside human attention: the orphan is found and held in view by God.
terra: The repeated divine finding continues from the orphan of 93:6 to one in need of guidance whom God guides, reinforcing the section's claim that the overlooked person remains found by God.
terra: God finds the Prophet in need and enriches him, continuing 93:6's repeated divine finding and supplying the provision that human neglect delays.

luna: The command “as for the orphan, do not oppress him” directly reverses the section's image of pushing the orphan and makes the orphan's treatment a test of response. | terra: فلا تقهر turns God's sheltering of the orphan in 93:6 into a direct command against overpowering him, the clearest reversal of يدع اليتيم.

luna: The adjoining command not to repel a petitioner extends the same refusal to push away a vulnerable person; 93:9 itself names the orphan. | terra: Do not rebuke the petitioner extends 93:9's care from the orphan to another person easily pushed away, and answers the missing food and closed hand in the section.
terra: Speaking of the Lord's favor follows commands about the orphan and petitioner; it distinguishes grateful testimony centered on the giver from display centered on oneself.
terra: Human transgression begins when a person sees himself as self-sufficient in 96:7, the same self-magnifying stance that pushes prayer and weaker people from view.
terra: Seeing oneself as self-sufficient supplies the false visual judgment behind the transgression named in 96:6 and the obstruction of prayer later in the passage.
terra: In the context of a man obstructing a servant's prayer, “Does he not know that God sees?” places divine sight over both prayer and performative human power.
terra: Sincere worship of God, prayer, and almsgiving are stated together, directly reversing prayer performed for an audience and care that never reaches the needy.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, reversing the human gaze that misses small persons, small gifts, and unobtrusive acts.
terra: An atom's weight of evil will likewise be seen, so neglect hidden beneath a respectable exterior cannot remain unseen.
terra: Rivalry for abundance distracts people until the graves, a compact account of attention captured by what is socially bright and countable.
